title: Backpressure
summary: What to do when work arrives faster than it can be done for longer than a queue can absorb: grow, reject, or slow the sender down.

blocks.p: A queue absorbs a short burst. But if work keeps arriving faster than consumers finish it, the queue grows without end. Every message waits longer than the one before.
Eventually the queue runs out of memory or disk, or messages wait so long that the result is useless. Nobody wants a password reset email an hour later. The system has to push back on the sender.
**Backpressure** is a signal from a busy stage to the stage feeding it: slow down. The first step is to give the queue a limit. Then decide what happens when it is full.

list: **Reject.** New messages are refused while the queue is full. The sender gets an error straight away and can retry later or give up. Wait times stay bounded.
**Block.** The sender waits until there is space. Pressure moves back up the chain, to the sender and then to whatever feeds it.
**Grow.** No limit. Nothing is refused, but waits grow without bound, and memory with them.

blocks.caption: Two consumers handle about 4 messages a second. For 6 seconds, 6.5 a second arrive. With no limit the wait keeps growing. With a limit of 8, the queue either rejects messages or makes the producer wait.

blocks.p: While work arrives faster than it is done, the queue grows by the difference every second. A message that joins the end waits for everything in front of it.

blocks.caption: Messages waiting after an overload, and how long the newest one waits.

blocks.p: This is why a limit matters. A bounded queue turns a long overload into some errors now, rather than slow answers for everyone later.

list: **TCP has backpressure built in.** The receiver advertises a window, the bytes it can accept. When its buffer fills the window shrinks and the sender stops, as [RFC 9293](https://www.rfc-editor.org/rfc/rfc9293) describes.

**Node.js streams signal it.** In Node.js, `write()` returns `false` when a stream's buffer is full, and the writer should wait for the `drain` event. See the [backpressuring in streams](https://nodejs.org/en/learn/modules/backpressuring-in-streams) guide.
**Reactive Streams makes the consumer ask.** In [Reactive Streams](https://www.reactive-streams.org/), a subscriber requests a number of items, and the publisher never sends more than requested.
**HTTP APIs reject.** A web service can't block its clients for long. It returns `429` or `503`, often with `Retry-After`, as in the rate limiting and load shedding lessons.
A queue only helps with bursts. A sustained overload makes it grow forever.
Give every queue a limit, and choose what happens when it is full.
Rejecting keeps waits short and tells the sender at once. Blocking moves the pressure back to the sender.
An unbounded queue hides an overload until waits, or memory, run out.

grow.label: No limit
grow.note: nothing refused, but waits keep growing
